title: This world is hau
hookLine: na na na, hey hey. songs everywhere carry syllables that mean nothing. the Sama Veda's chants have them too, and the Chandogya gives them a world
carry: upasana: seeing the whole world in the rite
tomorrow: what does the song rest on?
last: THE SONG RIDES ON THE BREATH.

cards: Na na na na. Hey hey. Ooh, la la.
Plenty of songs have a stretch where the words run out and the singer keeps going anyway. Nobody looks those syllables up. And yet a crowd of strangers will sing them back, louder than the verses.
Sama Veda chant has syllables like that too, sounds slipped between the words of the verse to carry the melody. A reader could skip them as filler. The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't.
Today: the sounds between the words.

teach.b: When a verse becomes a saman, a Sama Veda chant, the words don't stay as they were. Vowels stretch. Syllables repeat.
And between them come extra sounds, with names like hau and hai and auhoyi. These are stobhas. On their own they don't mean anything the way a word does; they're there for the song.
Then the Chandogya gives the stobhas the world.

teach.h: THIS WORLD IS HAU. THE WIND IS HAI.
teach.b: In paraphrase: this world is the sound hau. The wind is hai. The moon is atha.
And it goes on down a list, pairing chant-sounds with fire, with the sun, with breath, with food.

teach.h: UPASANA: THE WHOLE WORLD IN A SMALL SOUND.
teach.b: So the sounds a hurried listener would call filler, the Upanishad treats as the places where the whole world comes into the song.

This is a way of worship the Upanishads teach again and again, called upasana, literally a sitting near: meditating on one part of a rite as something greater. The singer doesn't only sound hau; he holds this world in it.
Readers take it more than one way. Some hear a meditation, a way to keep the whole world in mind while chanting.
Some hear a point about sound itself: in Hindu practice a sacred sound can matter even where it carries no dictionary meaning, and Vedic chanters still learn every syllable by ear and keep it exact.
Either way, the Chandogya refuses to throw the small sounds away. In this teaching, nothing in a rite is too small to hold the world.

how: In Sama Veda chanting, the words of a verse are stretched and repeated and joined by syllables called stobhas, and the chants are learned from a teacher by ear.

games.q: what does “the sama veda as song” mean?
o: a chant with every filler syllable taken out
a chant whose words are sung exactly as written
a chant whose small sounds carry the whole world

games.q: the sounds between the words — tap the pairs.
p: a chant-sound with no word meaning

s: in Sama Veda chant, the words are sung exactly as written
vowels stretch, syllables repeat, and stobhas come in between.
the Chandogya treats the stobhas as filler to skip
it pairs them with the world: this world is hau, the wind is hai.
a stobha doesn't mean anything the way a word does
it's there for the song, which is why the Chandogya's pairing is surprising.

games.q: you're chanting a saman and you reach hau. the Chandogya teaches upasana here. what does the singer do?
o: sing it while holding this world in mind
swap it for a real word
games.why: that's upasana: meditating on one part of the rite as something greater. hau is this world, hai the wind, atha the moon.

practice: On the out-breath let a soft open sound come, like haa or hau, quiet enough that no one else hears, just a sound with no meaning.

On the next breaths make the same sound and let it hold one thing each time, the ground under you, the air in the room; if silence suits the place you're in, make the sound inside. If you pray, let it be prayer.

wordCard.voice: The Sama Veda as song. In the chant, small sounds called stobhas carry the melody, and the Chandogya meditates on them as the world: upasana. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a syllable added in Sama Veda chant, outside the words of the verse.

carryVoice: Your line: upasana, seeing the whole world in the rite. Even in the small sounds. Same time tomorrow.
